speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Criminals are also becoming increasingly sophisticated and even more technologically savvy young adults are falling prey to these scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On the human level, the suffering caused by such scams is devastating.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As Members of Parliament, we see too many residents who have lost large sums, in the hundreds of thousands of dollars.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In most cases, lost monies are unlikely to be recovered.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The losses suffered by each victim are not just measured in monetary terms, that is, how much was lost; but also measured by the impact of that loss on the individual or the family, on persons with serious health issues, on retirees, on those with mouths to feed, on the vulnerable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: When it comes to scams, the Government and, in particular, the Monetary Authority of Singapore (MAS) has consistently said that it expects banks to treat its customers fairly.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Well, what exactly does the MAS expect of banks and how does it exercise its supervisory power?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For the customers, what recourse or support does the Government provide to them?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That is the focus of my Motion today.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a Straits Times opinion piece last Thursday, 14 September, technology editor Irene Tham opined that in order to fight scams, we may have to ditch some practices that make transactions easy.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: She pointed out that among others, banks needed to start accepting more responsibility.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Consumers too may have to put up with some inconvenience to keep online dealings secure.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In my view, the Government, as the regulator, also needs to step up.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Before I proceed further, it is only fair to acknowledge the efforts by multiple agencies to address the scourge of scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Among these efforts, the most visible are the scaled up public education and the setting up of the Anti-Scam Command and Anti-Scam Centre, with collaboration between law enforcement and banks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I have also come across cases where banks managed to contact customers quickly and were able to stop a transaction before it was completed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: But such success is, I believe, relatively rare.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This was the latest update to the House after pushing back the publication date for more than a year, citing the complexity of the issues.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: No doubt one such issue is likely the wide typology of scam victims, from those who are tricked by half-baked schemes to the tech savvy who inadvertently loaded malware onto their phones.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, the first clarification I would like to seek is – is the time frame for releasing the consultation by third quarter of this year, that is, by this month or two weeks from now, still on track?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If it is not, then what is causing the delay and by when can the paper be released?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First and fundamentally, consumers are not sufficiently equipped to combat scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Fraudsters have become increasingly sophisticated and can now take control of a customer's phone and obtain their bank login details through the clicking of a malicious link.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Even the most technologically savvy person could easily make this mistake and within a day, have their life savings wiped out.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While education and outreach efforts may go some way to mitigating this, it will always be playing catch up with these organised criminals.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With their increasing sophistry, targeting prey through social engineering, does the targeted person really stand a chance?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Second, deciding in each case what is equitable will take time and may be irrelevant to the more vulnerable in our society.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For a family whose life savings have been wiped out, this would be an inordinate and stressful delay.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Further, forcing certain vulnerable groups such as the elderly to confront a big bank would be far from ideal.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On a practical level, it would be difficult for them to gather and present evidence to prove that they have taken necessary precautions as will be required by the MAS.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Lastly, as to who should lead in combating scams, banks are best positioned and the best resourced to do so.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Therefore, banks should take an outsized role in preventing them.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Banks are able to monitor transactions, block suspicious payment flows and keep abreast of the latest technological developments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such endeavours are beyond the remit of most bank customers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Having emphasised why the banks should take the lead in combating scams, I shall move on to three policy solutions the Government should consider.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The first suggestion looks at how some other jurisdictions are protecting consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The second deals with some additional safeguards that the Government should require of banks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, I will argue why the Government should not take a hands-off approach when banks enter settlement agreements with affected customers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, policy suggestions and what some other jurisdictions are doing to protect consumers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This will apply except in cases where the customer was fraudulent or grossly negligent or the transaction involved cryptocurrency or international payments.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The solution for such mandatory reimbursement is simpler and quicker.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It is noteworthy that the UK is a major financial centre and is prepared to take this tough stance against the banks.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Australia is also reportedly considering adopting similar measures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Meanwhile, the European Commission (EC) too has moved on this.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In July this year, the EC proposed granting a refund to victims of authorised push payment fraud in certain circumstances as part of revisions to the EU payments directive.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It could cover all transfers between banks in Singapore via the FAST and PayNow systems.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Like the UK system, it could be scoped to protect customers who are consumers, small businesses and charities.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This would give Singaporeans the confidence to transact using these methods without fear that their savings would be unknowingly syphoned off.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would also ensure that victims of these scams will be compensated in a timely manner without having to undergo a complex adjudication process.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As I mentioned earlier, banks are best placed to identify and detect suspicious transactions such as when a customer's bank account is emptied over a short time, transfer limits are quickly changed, and new payees are added.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A cost-benefit analysis by the UK Payment Systems Regulator has also shown that the reimbursement model would incentivise payment service providers to improve the detection and prevention of fraud.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This finding seems to resonate with banks who have been reimbursing customers who have been scammed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: According to a senior official of UK bank TSB, having to reimburse customers for online fraud has incentivised it to be more proactive in detecting and preventing scams from the outset, resulting in less fraud.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To state the obvious, prevention is preferable to reimbursement as it stops the problem at its root.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As more jurisdictions adopt such measures, international banks will not baulk at such requirements or see Singapore as an outlier if it adopted similar measures.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While the MAS did note that bank customers have the responsibility to take necessary precautions, it cautioned that compensation paid should not weaken the incentive for all to be vigilant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the point remains that individual responsibility alone is insufficient to combat these increasingly sophisticated and malicious scams.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: While there is a general presumption that the laws should not apply retrospectively, this is a specific instance where it should.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Court of Appeal has explained in the case of ABU vs Comptroller of Income Tax that retrospective legislation is undesirable because it imposes penalties or other disadvantages without fair warning and undermines expectations.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, I would argue that this would not apply here, given that banks have been put on notice since the MAS informed the banks of a desire to implement a loss-sharing framework in February 2022, or one and a half years ago.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Banks had also been consulted as part of the process as early as 2021, being part of the Payments Council.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Accordingly, I urge the Government to ensure that these victims will be allowed to have their claims adjudicated fairly under the framework.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, policy suggestion two – additional safeguards for bank customers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, most banks only offer these on request and have a digital token or SMS verification as the default option for 2FA.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This means that the mobile phone becomes the single source of vulnerability.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Should the phone be infected with malware, 2FA does not, in effect, act as a second degree of authentication.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As pointed out by Ms Irene Tham in her article last week, experts believe that it is time to resurrect hardware tokens, which are standalone devices apart from the phone.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: MAS should advise banks to promote the physical tokens as the default option.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I also asked the Government to consider implementing additional verification checks where a customer transfers money to bank accounts of entities associated with cryptocurrencies or digital payment tokens (DPTs).

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To be fair, the MAS has recognised the risk involved with DPTs and has sought to regulate consumer access to DPTs.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I urge them to further consider regulating transfers to bank accounts associated with DPT service providers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: DPTs carry a higher risk of dissipation and are more difficult to trace, especially when transferred to wallets around the globe.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Imposing mandatory delays, transfer limits and additional authentication could go a long way towards preventing customer monies from being siphoned off by fraudsters.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Added verification steps and longer mandatory waiting periods should also be implemented where the transaction involves a vulnerable client, such as an elderly or mentally impaired person.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Banks should adopt closer scrutiny over transactions from such accounts, mandating lower transfer limits and longer waiting times by default.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For all these measures, banks can provide customers the option to opt out of these safeguards provided that they are sufficiently aware of the risk.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, policy solution three – safeguarding customers from unfair settlements.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: First, the sums offered as goodwill payments may be paltry in relation to the loss.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, such offers are usually tied to non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) which are onerous and one-sided, requiring absolute secrecy from the customer and requiring the customer to forgo all rights to recover further sums.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The one-sidedness of such arrangements was also alluded to by Member Yeo Wan Ling in a Parliamentary Question filed in November last year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, the unequal bargaining power between the banks and consumers is obvious.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Will the MAS stand by if desperate customers are being bulldozed and bullied?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: A hands-off approach by the MAS is unacceptable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: On this issue, please let me elaborate in Chinese.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: (In Mandarin):   When bank customers complain to their banks of the amount they lost to fraud, some banks will only offer them a small amount to solve the issue.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, such offers are usually tied to signing an agreement of non-disclosure (NDAs) by the customer.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This means that these customers are giving up their right to recover further sums in future.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The unequal bargaining power between the banks and consumers is obvious from this situation.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The Government should not take a hands-off approach.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Instead, the Government should roll out regulations for banks to comply with.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: (In English): Sir, while I agree that the MAS cannot micromanage the banks, can it do more than issue a motherhood statement that MAS expects the banks to treat their customers fairly?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At present, banks in Singapore have published a voluntary Code of Consumer Banking Practice.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Under paragraph 3B of the Code, fairness is a key principle in resolving a dispute between the consumer and the bank.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Customers should also be given full disclosure about their rights and forms of recourse against the bank.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a limit discourages those who have lost more from going to FIDReC.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such a revision to FIDReC's monetary limit —

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Ms Lim, you have under a minute left.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Of paramount importance is ensuring that Singaporeans have confidence in their banking system and ensuring that those who have suffered a loss are fairly compensated.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I have also highlighted why requiring customers to bear losses when they were not grossly negligent would not be fair.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: I urge the Government to do its part to ensure that we do right by bank customers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I share her concerns over losses suffered from scams, as do other Members in this House.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Over the past year, Dr Tan Wu Meng and Ms Yeo Wan Ling have raised questions on the avenues of recourse for customers who suffer losses from scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Mr Saktiandi Supaat and Dr Lim Wee Kiak also asked about the status of the Shared Responsibility Framework.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I will then share the avenues that customers have for recourse and provide an update on the Shared Responsibility Framework.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Singapore adopts a three-pronged strategy to fight scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: First, upstream measures, such as the ScamShield mobile app to filter and block scam messages and calls, and the SMS Sender ID Registry regime to label non-registered senders with the “Likely-SCAM” label.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Second, downstream measures, these include bank measures implemented last year.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And third, public education through public advisories and sharing best practices to fight scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Our collective efforts are showing some encouraging signs.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: With more of us transacting digitally, bad actors are adopting increasingly sophisticated methods to target victims.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We must constantly sharpen our approach to fight scams in this rapidly evolving landscape.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Among scam types prevalent today, digitally enabled scams involving phishing and malware are of gravest concern.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This is where victims either gave away or had their banking credentials stolen, leading to unauthorised transactions.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In recent months, we have seen a growing number of malware-enabled scam cases, with some victims suffering considerable losses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Left unaddressed, such scam threats and ensuing losses can undermine public confidence in payments and digital banking.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The Government is resolute in fighting malware-enabled scams, and we have augmented our efforts under the three prongs I mentioned.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore (CSA) and Singapore Police Force (SPF) are working with key tech players to limit mainstream access to identified malware variants and tools, such as those used in scams seen here in Singapore.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Agencies are also working with industry and international partners to raise the security standards of mobile operating systems and mobile devices.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: SPF has taken timely enforcement action, and works with banks to trace and recover funds.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: SPF also collaborates with overseas law enforcement agencies to take down cross-border scam syndicates.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: MAS has also been working closely with our banks to strengthen anti-malware controls, fraud surveillance, and detection capabilities.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Major retail banks have hence enhanced the security measures to protect customers against malware scams and will progressively introduce refinements or new measures to keep pace with changes in the threat landscape.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Members might know that the Association of Banks in Singapore (ABS) announced this a few hours ago.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: This will further help to limit losses against scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Members of the public must take active steps to protect themselves against scams.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We must foster stronger adoption of scam prevention actions and cyber hygiene practices through public engagements.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: SPF, CSA, MoneySENSE and banks have used multiple platforms such as outreach events, social and print media, as well as digital display panels to broadcast simple advisories, including messages such as "download only from official app stores" to the public.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: To the Member's point, the Government is also targeting outreach and messages to vulnerable groups, including seniors, students and migrant workers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: I will now address the matter that she raised about who should be responsible for scam losses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: And I think the House understands that this is a difficult issue, since amounts lost in any single case can be substantial.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We must, hence, strike a balance between fairness, accountability and compassion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: There are some views that banks can easily absorb losses arising from individual scam cases.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: However, full restitution without due consideration of culpability is neither fair nor desirable.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Doing so can erode vigilance and personal responsibility and lull users into complacency.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim suggested that customers rely on banks to ensure the security and the robustness of their online banking and payment options.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: However, we should also note that scammers can still bypass these digital security measures, by deceiving customers into inadvertently divulging their account access credentials or downloading malware, thereby granting scammers remote access to victims’ devices and their accounts.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Individual customers thus also have an important responsibility to protect access to their accounts and this includes practising good cyber hygiene and being diligent in preventing their login information and one-time passwords (OTPs) from being divulged to third parties.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: MAS has issued guidance for banks to institute clear customer handling and investigation processes and to treat customers fairly in all disputes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: MAS also monitors how banks handle such disputes.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: In scam cases, banks must consider if they have fulfilled their obligations, and whether the victim had acted responsibly.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Depending on the facts of each case, banks may offer goodwill payments to customers.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: If a customer is unsatisfied with an offer, he may decline and approach FIDReC for mediation and adjudication.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: A customer can further pursue his case in court if he is not satisfied with the outcome.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: If the customer accepts a goodwill payment offer, he or she will be bound by the terms of the offer.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Should new information come to light that is materially different from the premise upon which the customer had accepted the goodwill offer, the customer can request the bank to relook the case, or to approach FIDReC for assistance.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim pointed out that some other countries, including the United Kingdom, have either implemented or are considering mechanisms to mitigate the burden of scam losses.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: We are monitoring these developments, and will take them into account as we further develop this framework, including for other types of scams in the digital payments ecosystem.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Ms Sylvia Lim also talked about the physical token.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Customers can request for physical tokens and MAS is also looking at her suggestion.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On the other part about the digital payment tokens or crypto currency, I wanted to say that MAS also continues to watch for developments in the digital payment tokens or crypto-currency space, and will regularly review the adequacy and appropriateness of these regulations.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: On her point of FIDReC, FIDReC will also continue to monitor and regularly review its process and procedures.

speaker: The Minister of State for Culture, Community and Youth and Trade and Industry (Mr Alvin Tan)
text: Again, I thank Ms Sylvia Lim and Members in this House for their focus on this very important and rapidly evolving issue and I welcome all of you to work with the Government, to join us in our ongoing fight against scams.
